output.brief: The rise in chilled write-offs is mostly an internal problem, not a Haverlow problem. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four on 27 July, night pallets wait about 3h50 on average before reaching a chamber, up from 44 minutes. The dock is unrefrigerated and ran 15–17°C overnight. Night-received lots now have a 2.9% write-off rate, up from 0.6%, and this holds for every supplier. Day-shift rates are flat. Haverlow's trailer records show product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors opened, with no trend. The chambers held temperature. So the warm receiving probe readings reflect product that had already warmed on the dock. They do not show warm product arriving. I'm quite sure of this. A chargeback and a volume shift would punish the wrong party. Dropping the night probe would hide the problem. Lead with restoring night receiving to six and setting a maximum dock-to-chamber time, tracked weekly. Separately, reconcile a sample of Corriebank's claims. Self-certified credits rose from 3 August, but whether any claims are unwarranted is unproven. Don't reinstate photo evidence until that sample is reconciled.
